description: Preserves the tactic of pairing a progression pyramid with two tall side arrows that encode inverse trends rising toward opposite ends. This lets a single canvas convey both the staged hierarchy and the trade-off between two moving variables.
content: When a pyramid represents an evolution or progression, add a tall upward arrow on the left labeled with the qualities that increase toward the apex (e.g., instability/vulnerability) and a tall downward arrow on the right labeled with the qualities that increase toward the base (e.g., stability/resilience); use distinct muted arrow colors (light blue, lavender) so they read as annotations, not tiers, and stack multi-word labels along the arrow direction.
when_to_use: Use whenever a pyramid or tiered diagram needs to communicate not just stage hierarchy but also two opposing gradients or trade-offs that vary along its vertical axis.

title: Bilateral annotation rails for tiered pyramids
description: Preserves the pattern of flanking a multi-tier pyramid with two complementary side rails: color-coded guiding questions on the left and vision/zone labels on the right. Each tier thus reads as the answer to its question while the central content stays uncluttered.
content: Align one guiding question per tier on the left at the tier's vertical center (color-code each question to its tier), and place tier vision labels (WHY/WHAT/HOW) on the right; render inter-tier dividers as labeled dashed lines (e.g., 'Allocation relations') and add zone markers like OUTSIDE/INSIDE beside the topmost boundary.
when_to_use: When a pyramid or layered diagram must convey both per-level content and the top-down narrative/rationale linking levels, such as architecture visions or strategy-to-execution mappings.

title: Side-bracket superordinate grouping
description: Preserves the technique of overlaying a secondary categorical hierarchy onto a pyramid by placing vertical grouping brackets in a dedicated right-side gutter, keeping tier interiors uncluttered.
content: Reserve a right-side margin (roughly 15-20% of canvas width) and draw one vertical square bracket per group, with bracket endpoints aligned exactly to the outer edges of the first and last tier it spans; place each group label at the bracket's vertical midpoint, ordered so brackets read top-to-bottom in the same sequence as the groups they cover.
when_to_use: When a pyramid (or stacked-layer diagram) needs tiers grouped into higher-level categories in addition to their individual labels.

title: Alt-Fragment Branching for Mutually Exclusive Outcomes
description: Preserves the tactic of modeling a decision point with two or more mutually exclusive results as a single 'alt' combined fragment with one operand per outcome, rather than drawing unconditional parallel messages.
content: When a flow diverges (e.g., valid vs invalid login), wrap the diverging messages in one alt fragment spanning exactly the lifelines involved; split it with a dashed horizontal separator, guard each operand with a bracketed condition like [Login Valid], and place exactly the outcome's message(s) inside its operand while keeping the shared trigger (Verify) above the fragment.
when_to_use: Use for sequence diagrams where a request leads to distinct conditional response paths (success/failure, found/not-found, authorized/denied).

title: Canonical repeated interaction block per operation
description: Preserves the tactic of modeling each user operation as an identical three-lifeline exchange (actor request → system forwards to database → self-check → dashed returns back through the chain), so many similar operations read as clean stacked repetitions of one block.
content: For each actor operation, emit the same block: solid arrow Actor→System, solid arrow System→Database, optional self-message on Database, then dashed 'Response' Database→System and dashed 'Display message' System→Actor; reuse identical return labels ('Response', 'Display message') and vary only the initiating request label per block.
when_to_use: When a sequence diagram spec lists many homogeneous admin/CRUD-style operations against the same system and database lifelines.

title: Flow-Ordered Lifelines with Numbered Messages
description: Preserves the sample's tactic of ordering lifelines left-to-right to mirror the dominant call direction and numbering every message so the diagram reads top-to-bottom as a single traceable scenario.
content: Place the external actor at the far left, then arrange internal lifelines in the order they are invoked (e.g., Operators → CPN Controller → ANN Inputs Controller → Farm Details → ANN Outputs Controller) so most arrows point rightward with minimal crossing; label each message with a sequential number, use dashed return arrows for success/error outcomes, and model validations as self-messages (e.g., 'Workflow successful?') with activation bars only on active lifelines.
when_to_use: When a user requests a sequence diagram with many lifelines (5+) and an explicitly numbered or step-wise message flow describing one end-to-end business scenario.

title: Horizontal spine with stacked feedback return loops
description: Preserves the layout pattern for system/flow diagrams that combine a main left-to-right process chain with multiple feedback loops returning to an upstream decision node.
content: Place the primary flow on a single horizontal spine (inputs converge → decision → process → outputs → fanned-out outcome boxes stacked vertically at the right), then route each feedback loop on its own horizontal band above or below the spine, inserting a labeled box mid-loop so the loop's meaning is readable as text on the path back to the decision node.
when_to_use: Use when a state/flowchart diagram has one dominant forward pipeline plus two or more labeled feedback loops (e.g., positive/negative, equilibrium/disequilibrium) that must return to an earlier node without crossing or cluttering the main flow.

title: Composite region with internal initial and boundary exit
description: Preserves how to model a convergent sub-lifecycle in a UML state machine: group the inner states into one named composite region and route abnormal global exits from the region border rather than from individual inner states.
content: When multiple top-level states (e.g., Composed via [Send], Save via [Send]) funnel into the same multi-stage flow, draw that flow as a composite state with a tab label in its top-left corner, give it its own internal initial pseudostate chaining into the first inner state, and attach exceptional exits (e.g., 'Account Limit Reached [HighPriority] /SendMessage' -> Archived) to the region's outer edge. Use full 'trigger [guard] /effect' labels on such transitions to encode UML semantics explicitly.
when_to_use: A state machine diagram where several entry transitions converge on a shared sub-flow that also has region-wide exceptional exits.

title: Hub-spoke visual hierarchy with externalized captions and decoding legend
description: Preserves a proven styling scheme for hub-and-spoke diagrams: a high-contrast central hub, uniform lighter satellite nodes, muted edge labels, italic sub-captions carrying detail outside the circles, and a legend that decodes the color/typography encoding.
content: Render the hub in a dark saturated fill (e.g., navy) with bold white text, all spokes in one lighter tint of the same hue with dark text, and arrows in neutral gray with short verb-phrase labels; place multi-item details as italic gray captions beneath each spoke circle instead of inside it, and add a small legend box mapping 'colored circle = category A' and 'italic caption = category B'.
when_to_use: Use for hub-and-spoke/radial diagrams where one central concept connects to several peer nodes that each carry secondary list-like details and the viewer needs an explicit key to the visual encoding.

title: Backward rejection path with merge-back edges
description: Preserves how this sample topologically organizes multi-decision swimlanes: the happy path advances forward across lanes (left-to-right, top-to-bottom) while rejection branches form a distinct backward return path (right-to-left) through the lanes responsible for rework/notification, and recovery branches rejoin existing nodes instead of duplicating them.
content: Route each decision's YES branch forward to the next stage and place NO branches on a separate lower/backtrack row flowing right-to-left through the responsible lanes (e.g., Construction -> Contracts -> Sales), ending at the notifier node. When a later decision rejoins the main flow (e.g., 'Terms accepted?' YES), draw an upward edge into the already-placed downstream node rather than creating a duplicate.
when_to_use: When a swimlane activity diagram has approval/review decisions whose rejection triggers rework, delay, or notification steps owned by earlier lanes.

title: Row-Banded Branch Separation for Swimlane Loops
description: Preserves the spatial plan that kept this five-lane workflow readable: the forward 'happy path' and the rejection/rework loop occupy separate horizontal bands so arrows never cross.
content: Assign the main start-to-end flow (start node → chained processes → Yes branches → end node) to the top row of the lanes, and route every No/rework branch (e.g., 'Terms accepted? No → return files → delayed → notify client') along a dedicated lower row, connecting bands with short vertical arrows inside the responsible lane. Keep each decision diamond in the lane of the deciding actor, send forward flow left-to-right/downward, and send loop-back flow leftward only within the lower band.
when_to_use: Multi-lane swimlane activity diagrams where decision diamonds produce both a forward continuation and a backward rework/rejection loop spanning several lanes.

title: Mid-height merge node with bottom-routed rejection backflow
description: Preserves how to lay out converging decision branches and cross-lane rework loops in a swimlane activity diagram so that forward and backward flows never tangle or duplicate nodes.
content: Place the shared convergence node (e.g., 'Construction starts') at an intermediate vertical position so the happy path enters it from above and the approved-rework path enters with a short upward arrow from below; route the rejection chain (Construction → Contracts → Sales, right-to-left) along a lower band beneath the main left-to-right flow so backward edges run parallel under, and never cross, forward edges.
when_to_use: Swimlane or activity diagrams with multiple decision diamonds whose branches reconverge on one node, or where a NO/rejection branch must flow backward across lanes to earlier-stage lanes.

title: Central color-echoed ring anchoring a 2x2 quadrant grid
description: A radial SWOT composition where a central ring, split into four arcs color-matched to each quadrant, acts as the visual hub, while text blocks and corner badges radiate outward to reinforce grouping and reading order.
content: Place four rounded-square panels in a 2x2 grid around a central circular ring divided into four arcs, each arc colored to match its corresponding quadrant; put a diagonal ribbon with a white letter badge (S/W/O/T) on each panel's OUTER corner, an icon inside the panel, and the bold heading plus description paragraph on the panel's OUTER side (left for left column, right for right column).
when_to_use: Use for SWOT or any four-part quadrant analysis where categories need strong color-coded identity, a clear S→W→O→T reading flow, and a central thematic icon anchoring the composition.

title: Alternating-side anchor blocks in stacked bands
description: Preserves the zigzag band pattern used in this vertical SWOT: four stacked horizontal rows where the solid colored letter square alternates sides (S left, W right, O left, T right) against a bordered text panel, creating visual rhythm without breaking the strict top-to-bottom reading order.
content: When stacking N repeated horizontal bands (one per quadrant/item), keep each band structurally identical (colored square with white letter + adjacent bordered text panel of fixed height) but flip the anchor block to the opposite side on alternate rows; maintain consistent band heights, gutter spacing, and border/accent color so the alternation reads as intentional rhythm rather than inconsistency.
when_to_use: Use for vertical SWOT or similar multi-quadrant templates (Pestle, 4-section frameworks) where the user requests stacked bands and wants visual variety while preserving sequential reading flow.

title: Center-Hub Overlap with Mirrored Quadrant Anchors
description: Preserves how this SWOT sample unifies a 2x2 matrix: a large title circle placed exactly over the quadrant intersection acts as a visual hub, while badge/label pairs are mirrored left-to-right across quadrants for balance.
content: For 2x2 matrix diagrams, place a large circle (filled with the darkest palette color) centered precisely on the quadrant intersection and stack the diagram title inside it on two lines. Then mirror each quadrant's anchor elements: badge-then-label on left-side quadrants, label-then-badge right-aligned on right-side quadrants, so all four corners feel symmetric around the hub.
when_to_use: Use when generating 2x2 matrix templates (SWOT, Eisenhower, BCG-style grids) that need a strong central anchor and clean symmetry without connectors.

title: Serpentine row-wrapping for dense timelines
description: Preserves the S-shaped folding pattern that lets a long chronological sequence (10 nodes) fit on one canvas while keeping a single unbroken connector and unambiguous reading order. Also captures the per-row label mirroring that prevents text from colliding with the winding line.
content: Split nodes into horizontal rows that alternate flow direction (left-to-right, then right-to-left, then left-to-right), joining them with one continuous thin connector that curves down at each row end. Keep node anatomy identical (colored circle, white pictogram, bold year, short caption) but mirror label anchoring per row so years sit on the incoming-flow side and captions hang below, clear of the connector.
when_to_use: Use when a timeline has too many events (roughly 7 or more) to remain legible on a single straight horizontal or vertical axis.

title: Alternating mirrored annotation columns around a central spine
description: For vertical timelines with many nodes, this sample balances dense per-node content by splitting each node's annotation into two mirrored blocks: the bold label + date range on one side of the spine and an italic theme phrase + bullet list on the opposite side, alternating sides node to node.
content: Place each node's primary label (bold name + date range) on alternating left/right sides of the central vertical line, and put the secondary annotation (italic theme phrase plus indented bullet list) on the opposite side of the same node, connecting both with short horizontal connector lines so each era is read as a left+right pair.
when_to_use: Vertical timeline with 6+ nodes where each node carries both a title/date and supplementary text or bullet lists that would overcrowd a single side.

title: Gantt timeline with era bands and shared gridline axis
description: Preserves the layout system that made this timeline readable: a bottom time axis with uniform tick intervals, full-height vertical gridlines, and a top header row of era columns that partition the same horizontal scale.
content: Place the year axis at the bottom with equal-interval ticks (e.g., 20 years), draw thin vertical gridlines up from each tick across the canvas, and align a colored era-header row on top so each era column spans its exact tick range; render each entry as a horizontal bar spanning its start–end years, stacking bars at increasing vertical offsets to prevent overlap, and push supplementary detail (sub-style lists, captions) into a bottom-corner footnote legend keyed by an asterisk on the relevant bar.
when_to_use: Use whenever a Gantt-style or multi-era timeline must show many overlapping date spans against one continuous time scale, especially when entries group into named eras and some need enumerated sub-items.

title: Depth-role color coding for semantic trees
description: Preserves the sample's consistent color-by-semantic-role system that keeps a dense linguistic tree scannable: each tree depth/function gets its own hue, while connectors stay neutral.
content: Assign fixed node colors by role/depth (red = root's main branches, green = sub-meanings/senses, blue = leaf explanations/notes, purple small dots = word forms/synonym hubs), render all edges as thin gray lines, and use a light background; keep purple nodes small/dot-like so synonym starbursts read as secondary annotations rather than primary structure.
when_to_use: When building radial or left-to-right semantic/syntax tree mind maps with 4+ node categories (branches, senses, explanations, synonyms) that must remain legible at high node counts.

title: Columnar cause-and-effect map with selective connectivity
description: Organizes a cause-and-effect diagram as labeled category columns of sticky-note boxes rather than a strict hierarchy, with causal arrows crossing columns to show how problem domains interrelate. Preserves the choice to leave nodes unconnected when no relationship is stated.
content: Group nodes into vertical columns under bold uppercase category headers, then draw causal arrows horizontally (or diagonally) across columns between related notes; render uncertain relationships as dashed arrows annotated with '?' and deliberately leave any node with no specified relationship unconnected instead of forcing links.
when_to_use: The user requests a cause-and-effect or problem-analysis diagram organized into explicitly named categories (e.g., themed columns) with some specified and some uncertain relationships.

title: Color-code node semantics with an explicit legend
description: This sample preserves the tactic of assigning distinct fill colors to semantically different node types (yellow = decision/Test, orange = terminal/Outcome) and pairing the encoding with a legend box so the color meaning is self-documenting.
content: When a diagram contains two or more semantic node categories, assign each category a consistent, visually distinct fill color (e.g., yellow for internal decision nodes, orange for terminal outcome nodes), apply it uniformly across all nodes of that type, and place a small legend box (colored swatch + label) in a free corner of the canvas explaining each color.
when_to_use: Use whenever the user specifies (or the domain implies) categorical node types in a tree/flowchart—such as tests vs. outcomes, decisions vs. terminals, or states vs. actions—especially if the user requests a legend or color explanation.

title: Additive-blend overlap fills with white center
description: Preserves the technique of rendering Venn overlaps via additive color mixing (blue+yellow=green, blue+red=purple, yellow+red=orange) while reserving the triple intersection as white space for the key takeaway label.
content: Fill each Venn circle with a semi-transparent primary-like color (blue, yellow, red/pink) so pairwise overlaps naturally blend into secondary colors, and explicitly leave the central triple-overlap region white (or near-white) so the conclusion text there stands out in black; keep thin black circle outlines and black uppercase labels for legibility against saturated fills.
when_to_use: When building a multi-circle Venn diagram whose intersections carry meaning, especially when the center region must display an emphasized conclusion label.

title: Triangular three-circle Venn with full seven-zone item placement
description: Preserves the spatial recipe for a three-set Venn where every combination zone is populated: two circles on top, one centered below, so all pairwise-only overlaps and the triple overlap remain distinct, readable regions.
content: Arrange the three ellipses in a triangle (set A top-left, set B top-right, set C bottom-center) with roughly 40-50% pairwise overlap; then stack each item as centered multi-line text inside its exact zone—unique items near the outer crescent, pairwise-only items in the lens areas offset from center, and the triple-overlap item in the small central lens—shrinking font size for zones with multiple entries.
when_to_use: When a user requests a three-set Venn diagram specifying items for unique zones, all three pairwise-only intersections, and the central triple intersection.

title: Discrete zone-fills with numbered legend for Venn overlaps
description: Preserves the tactic of treating each Venn intersection as an individually styled zone (flat pastel fill + bold numeral + directional arrows) instead of relying on transparent circle blends, plus a swatch legend that decodes the numbers.
content: Fill each pairwise lens with its own flat, muted pastel and the central triple-overlap with a dark charcoal fill using reversed white marks for contrast; stamp every zone with a bold number, add small double-headed arrows in lenses (radiating arrows in the center) for visual interest, and mirror the exact swatches in a vertical side legend mapping numbers to meanings.
when_to_use: Multi-circle Venn diagrams where each intersection carries a distinct labeled meaning that must be referenced in a legend or keyed narrative, especially conceptual or humorous diagrams.

title: Canonical Notation Fidelity
description: Every diagram formalism has a mandated shape vocabulary; use it exactly and never substitute decorative or ad-hoc shapes for notation-defined primitives.
content: Before placing any element, identify the target notation and map each element category to its prescribed form: compartmented rectangles for classes with visibility markers and typed attributes, circles/rounded forms for processes, flat rectangles for external entities, open-ended stores for data, diamonds for decisions or composition, terminators, parallelograms, chevrons as specified. Render mandated adornments (stereotypes, multiplicities, filled diamonds, header bands) faithfully. If an element cannot be expressed in the notation, re-express the concept rather than inventing a shape.
when_to_use: Always, for any diagram belonging to a defined notation system (UML, DFD, flowchart, architecture, concept map); the check applies to every node and edge before styling begins.

title: Deterministic Role-to-Form Mapping
description: Each semantic role maps to exactly one visual form, held constant across the entire diagram; never blend idioms or let one form serve two meanings.
content: Define the full element taxonomy up front (entity, process, store, class, category level, annotation) and assign each a unique, unambiguous shape and line style: e.g., solid lines for one relationship type, dashed/dotted for another. Enforce the mapping globally — the same role drawn in two places must look identical, and two different roles must never share a form. Relationship types get distinct connector styles just as node types get distinct shapes.
when_to_use: Whenever a diagram contains two or more element or relationship categories; resolve the complete mapping before drawing any instances.

title: Complete Labeling of Nodes and Edges
description: Every element and every connector must carry an explicit textual identity — a name, and where applicable its formal role — so the diagram is machine-checkable and self-explanatory.
content: Label every node with its name (bold where primary) and role qualifier (stereotype, number, type); label every edge with its relationship or flow content; mark directionality on all flows with arrowheads. Use symbolic variable names, typed attributes, and correct mathematical typography where the content is formal rather than prose approximations. An unlabeled shape or line is treated as an error, not a stylistic choice.
when_to_use: Universally, at structure definition time; verify in a final pass that no node, edge, group, or container lacks an identifying label.

title: Single Dominant Visual Anchor
description: Establish exactly one primary element as the diagram's anchor — at the geometric center or top-center — so visual hierarchy mirrors conceptual hierarchy.
content: Identify the single most important artifact (root concept, central system, governing equation, primary process) and place it at the canonical anchor position: center for hub/star arrangements, top-center for hierarchies and flows. Make it the visually heaviest element (largest, darkest, or sole accent). All secondary elements position relative to it: satellites radiate around it, tiers descend below it, flows depart from or converge to it. Exactly one anchor per diagram — competing focal points destroy hierarchy.
when_to_use: Every diagram; decide the anchor first, before positioning anything else, regardless of whether the composition ends up radial, hierarchical, or linear.

title: One Consistent Reading Axis
description: Choose a single primary direction of reading aligned with the content's inherent ordering — and never violate it within the diagram.
content: Determine the content's natural sequence (chronology, value chain, causal flow, abstraction hierarchy, algorithm steps) and map it to one axis: left-to-right for timelines and pipelines, top-to-bottom for hierarchies and descending specificity, clockwise for cycles. Inputs/inbound elements enter from the start side (left/top), outputs exit at the end side (right/bottom). All primary flows run along the axis; secondary flows may branch but must not reverse the reading direction ambiguously. Number sequential steps explicitly.
when_to_use: Any diagram encoding sequence, flow, progression, or ranking; select the axis during layout planning and audit all connectors against it afterward.

title: Balanced Even Distribution of Satellites
description: Distribute secondary elements evenly and symmetrically around the anchor or along the flow so no region is crowded and no side is visually heavier.
content: Arrange peripheral nodes in balanced configurations: symmetric left/right columns, even radial spacing around a hub, or uniformly spaced tiers and ticks along an axis. Keep inter-node gaps consistent; mirror element counts across the midline where possible. Balance is compositional, not just geometric — equalize visual weight (size x color saturation) across regions, not merely node counts.

title: Modular Containment with Explicit Boundaries
description: Group related elements into labeled containers, bands, or frames with clear spatial separation between groups, so subsystem structure is visible at a glance.
content: Identify cohesive subsystems (layers, packages, phases, categories) and enclose each in a drawn boundary — labeled horizontal bands for layers, tabbed frames for packages, boundary boxes for system scope. Give every container its own label. Maintain exclusion zones: whitespace gutters between groups that no connector or node occupies casually; crossings between containers should be intentional, minimal, and routed orthogonally. External entities stay outside the boundary, internal parts inside.
when_to_use: Whenever the model has more than one subsystem, layer, phase, or category; essential for architectures, scoped systems, and multi-category compositions.

title: Restrained Palette on a Neutral Canvas with One Reserved Accent
description: Render on a plain light/white background with a minimal palette, and reserve exactly one vivid accent color for the single focal element or one designated highlight class.
content: Start from a white or near-white canvas. Build the palette from grayscale or one monochrome family plus muted fills; add at most one saturated accent (e.g., a single red volume or yellow border) assigned to the anchor or to one highlight/annotation class — never both, never scattered. Depth and emphasis come from soft shadows, outline weight, and spacing, not from additional hues. If a second vivid color seems necessary, encode the distinction by shape or line style instead.
when_to_use: Always as the default styling baseline; relax only when a category-coding scheme legitimately requires multiple hues, and even then keep saturation low and counts small.

description: When color encodes meaning, assign each category one distinct fill/outline color, keep it constant everywhere, and keep structural scaffolding neutral so the color semantics stay unambiguous.
content: Assign a unique color per semantic category (entity types, hierarchy levels, material families, flow paths) and apply it uniformly to every member of that category across the whole diagram. Keep containers, connectors, and arrows in neutral black/gray so they never compete with or contaminate the color code. Never reuse a category color for a different meaning or for decoration; never let annotation colors collide with structural colors. Node text stays dark and high-contrast against any fill.
when_to_use: Whenever the diagram has two or more semantic categories worth distinguishing; define the color legend alongside the role-to-form mapping before rendering.

title: Typographic Hierarchy Encodes Content Type
description: Use type weight and style to classify content — bold for primary labels and titles, regular for body text, italic for annotations and edge labels — and render formal symbols with full typographic fidelity.
content: Set the diagram title in large bold type at its canonical position; bold the pivotal terms and primary node labels; keep secondary node text regular; reserve italic strictly for flow labels, group headers, and contextual annotations so readers can classify any text at a glance. Render formal notation faithfully: superscripts/subscripts, Greek letters, operators, and symbolic variable names exactly as the discipline writes them. Never use italics decoratively or bold randomly — every typographic deviation must signal a content class.
when_to_use: Universally; apply after content placement, and audit that each text element's style matches its role (title, primary label, secondary label, annotation).

title: Legend for Compound Encodings
description: Whenever more than one visual encoding channel is active simultaneously (multiple shapes, colors, or line styles), include a legend that maps each style to its meaning.
content: After structure and styling are complete, enumerate every active encoding: node shapes, fill/outline colors, arrow and line styles, boundary types. If two or more channels coexist, add a compact legend in a consistent corner position mapping each visual style to its semantic role. Then verify the reverse: every style appearing in the diagram appears in the legend, and every legend entry is actually used. Single-notation diagrams with universally known symbols may omit it, but mixed or augmented idioms may not.
when_to_use: In the finalization pass of any diagram combining multiple notations, color-coded categories, or more than one connector style; mandatory for multi-encoding compositions.

title: Density Control and Annotation-Layer Separation
description: Cap visual density per region, preserve deliberate whitespace, and keep the annotation layer visually distinct from the structural layer so explanations never masquerade as model elements.
content: Audit the finished diagram: enforce even spacing, eliminate overlaps and unnecessary connector crossings, and split or abstract any region exceeding comfortable element counts (roughly 5-9 siblings per group). Maintain exclusion zones around the anchor and between modules. Render all explanatory content — notes, leader lines, contextual remarks — in a reserved style distinct from the structural encoding (e.g., dashed leaders, a single reserved annotation color, italic text), so annotation can never be confused with model structure. Remove redundant ink: shadows, grids, and decorations only where they aid depth or alignment.
when_to_use: As the final quality pass on every diagram, and iteratively whenever elements are added; especially critical for information-rich compositions with notes, highlights, or mixed audiences.
